WeAct: Dynamic Weight Switching as Agent Actions

Rui Shi* Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University
ruishi@andrew.cmu.edu    Xunjian Yin* Affiliation: Duke University
xunjian.yin@duke.edu    Jiacheng Sang* Affiliation: Duke University
jiacheng.sang@duke.edu    Zichuan Liu Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University
zichuanl@andrew.cmu.edu    Shuyan Zhou Affiliation: Duke University
Meta MSL
shuyan.zhou@duke.edu
Abstract

Long-horizon agents must learn heterogeneous capabilities from interleaved trajectories. Updating shared parameters to learn new capabilities can degrade previously acquired ones, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. As a trajectory unfolds, different stages may require different capabilities, yet conventional joint training and static adapter merging maintain a fixed parameter configuration throughout execution. We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions), which trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent’s action space. These internal actions use the model’s native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition in a shared context. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning counterparts despite using less compute, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method. WeAct also supports modular continual adaptation, by adding a new code computation adapter to expand the agent’s capabilities and updating the existing writing adapter to improve report quality. Both updates leave the backbone and other adapters unchanged, supporting modular continual adaptation in agents.

11footnotetext: Equal contribution.

1 Introduction

Long-horizon agents plan and invoke tools, connect evidence across sources and reasoning steps, and retrieve and synthesize web information over many turns. The required capabilities vary across stages and must adapt as domains, tools, and output requirements evolve. Fine-tuning or reinforcement learning (Li et al., 2026a; Hu et al., 2025) typically optimize these capabilities in shared parameters: misaligned capability gradients can impair joint learning (Li et al., 2026b), and later updates can erode earlier gains (Thede et al., 2026). Prompt-level skills (Ni et al., 2026) offer adaptation without changing weights, but their instructions consume context when loaded for execution.

Separate LoRA adapters isolate capability parameters, but their composition adds deployment requirements. MoLE (Wu et al., 2024) and LD-MoLE (Zhuang et al., 2026) mix expert outputs through layerwise gates, requiring support for composition inside the forward pass. Static merging, from conflict reduction in TIES (Yadav et al., 2023) to alignment in KnOTS (Stoica et al., 2025), combines updates before deployment. These methods improve composition, but use fixed merged weights across stages, which may weaken the specialization needed at each stage. Our key idea is to make independently maintained capabilities callable as agent actions. Extending ReAct’s external actions (Yao et al., 2023), we use internal actions to activate learned weights with on-demand flexibility.

We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions; Figure 1), a general method for capability composition in tool-using agents, to learn heterogeneous capabilities for long-horizon tasks while preserving prior gains and invoking the capability needed at each stage. Each capability LoRA is trained over a frozen backbone on its own stages and exit actions, using preceding interactions as context. It learns to continue prior work, reason, call tools, and hand back control. At inference, our load_lora and offload_lora tools activate and release one adapter through the native tool-calling interface, with their descriptions and control exchanges recorded in context. The selected weights govern subsequent reasoning and tool use within the same history. WeAct-soft chooses capabilities from this history; WeAct-hard prescribes loading every adapter in the workflow for reliable invocation. Both use the same interface without a separately trained router. Adding or refreshing a capability updates only its adapter.

Experiments on Qwen3-32B test capability separation during learning and execution. Controlled diagnostics show that extra shared capacity does not prevent lost gains and that tested static merges reduce specialists’ target-text fit (Section 3). Across eight deep-research benchmarks, WeAct-hard reaches 45.47% average accuracy, a 6.2% relative improvement over Full SFT, and both variants outperform all tested static merges on every benchmark (Section 4.2). WeAct uses fewer trainable parameters and less nominal training compute than Full SFT while retaining the evaluated general capabilities. Code insertion expands the library with stable performance, and Writing refresh improves report quality on ResearchQA and DeepResearchBench (Section 4.5). These results suggest potential for modular continual adaptation through capability expansion and local refinement.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We present WeAct for independent capability training and coordinated invocation via native tools in a shared history.

  • •

    We distinguish learning interference from static fusion mismatch, motivating capability-aligned training and intact adapter selection.

  • •

    We demonstrate improved deep-research performance alongside capability insertion and local refinement, supporting continual learning through modular expansion and updates.

2 Method

2.1 Preliminaries and Overview

Given a research query qq, an agent gathers evidence and answers through successive reasoning and tool interactions. We train capability adapters independently and select them as the task unfolds. Let θ0\theta_{0} denote a frozen language model’s parameters and {Δ​θk}k=1K\{\Delta\theta_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} a capability adapter library. Let ℳ\mathcal{M} index the linear maps adapted by LoRA. For a map ℓ∈ℳ\ell\in\mathcal{M} with input and output dimensions din,ℓd_{\mathrm{in},\ell} and dout,ℓd_{\mathrm{out},\ell}, LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) gives

Wk,ℓ=W0,ℓ+αkrk​Bk,ℓ​Ak,ℓ,Ak,ℓ∈ℝrk×din,ℓ,Bk,ℓ∈ℝdout,ℓ×rk.\begin{gathered}W_{k,\ell}=W_{0,\ell}+\frac{\alpha_{k}}{r_{k}}B_{k,\ell}A_{k,\ell},\\ A_{k,\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{k}\times d_{\mathrm{in},\ell}},\quad B_{k,\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out},\ell}\times r_{k}}.\end{gathered} (1)

Here rkr_{k} and αk\alpha_{k} are the rank and scaling coefficient. The trainable factors ϕk={Ak,ℓ,Bk,ℓ}ℓ∈ℳ\phi_{k}=\{A_{k,\ell},B_{k,\ell}\}_{\ell\in\mathcal{M}} determine Δ​θk=Δ​θk​(ϕk)\Delta\theta_{k}=\Delta\theta_{k}(\phi_{k}); different capabilities may use different ranks. We write πk=πθ0+Δ​θk\pi_{k}=\pi_{\theta_{0}+\Delta\theta_{k}} and set Δ​θ∅=0\Delta\theta_{\varnothing}=0 for base-only generation.

At step tt, history hth_{t} retains instructions, model turns, and tool outputs. With at most one adapter active, zt∈{∅,1,…,K}z_{t}\in\{\varnothing,1,\ldots,K\} selects the policy:

at∼πzt(⋅∣ht)=πθ0+Δ​θzt(⋅∣ht).a_{t}\sim\pi_{z_{t}}(\cdot\mid h_{t})=\pi_{\theta_{0}+\Delta\theta_{z_{t}}}(\cdot\mid h_{t}). (2)

ata_{t} may contain reasoning or tool calls; internal tool calls change ztz_{t} for subsequent generation.

Figure 2 connects training and inference. During training, stage-specific assistant targets and exit calls supervise independent adapters over retained execution context. We group deep-research stages into planning, evidence search and verification, and writing, yielding LoRA-plan, LoRA-search, and LoRA-write. These stages separate deciding what to do next, acquiring and checking external evidence, and synthesizing the answer. In exploratory annotation, finer splits were unstable: separating retrieval from verification or adding a state-recap stage let small rule changes move the same evidence operation between labels, and folding retrieval into planning made Plan absorb evidence-gathering steps (Appendix A.2). We therefore keep evidence operations together in LoRA-search. During inference, external tools supply observations and internal actions select weights, with both exchanges extending the shared history. WeAct-hard prescribes adapter invocation for reliable use; WeAct-soft selects capabilities according to the evolving task state in that history.

2.2 Capability Learning with Execution Context

Shared updates risk gradient interference and catastrophic forgetting. We isolate capability updates in separate adapters to prevent one capability from overwriting another’s parameters. Consider shared trainable parameters ω\omega and capability losses ℒjshared\mathcal{L}_{j}^{\mathrm{shared}}. With gi=∇ωℒishared​(ω)g_{i}=\nabla_{\omega}\mathcal{L}_{i}^{\mathrm{shared}}(\omega) for i∈{j,k}i\in\{j,k\}, a gradient step for capability kk changes capability jj’s loss to first order as

ℒjshared​(ω−η​gk)−ℒjshared​(ω)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{j}^{\mathrm{shared}}(\omega-\eta g_{k})-\mathcal{L}_{j}^{\mathrm{shared}}(\omega) (3)
=−η​gj⊤​gk+O⁡(η2),\displaystyle=-\eta\,g_{j}^{\top}g_{k}+O(\eta^{2}),

for a locally smooth loss and step size η\eta. The alignment and magnitude of these gradients determine the first-order interaction; Section 3 measures the resulting retention effects.

We define capabilities by stage function, each potentially spanning several assistant/tool exchanges. LoRA-plan develops goals and action plans; LoRA-search covers evidence acquisition, filtering, and verification; LoRA-write synthesizes evidence into an answer.

Each training sample retains preceding work so the module learns to continue an ongoing task. For capability kk, let pp be the retained preceding history, uku_{k} the loading call and result, ckc_{k} the stage’s interleaved assistant/tool content, and vkv_{k} its terminal assistant exit call. Concatenating these tokenized segments gives

s=p⊕uk⊕ck⊕vk=(x1,…,xN),mk,n=𝟏{n∈𝒜k(s)}.\begin{gathered}s=p\oplus u_{k}\oplus c_{k}\oplus v_{k}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}),\\ m_{k,n}=\mathbf{1}\{n\in\mathcal{A}_{k}(s)\}.\end{gathered} (4)

The set 𝒜k​(s)\mathcal{A}_{k}(s) contains the assistant-token positions used to supervise the current capability, including those corresponding to the exit call. The loss mask is zero for earlier assistant turns, the loading exchange, and tool observations. For the stage dataset 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k}, each module minimizes the objective:

ℒk(ϕk)=−𝔼s∼𝒟k∑n=1Nmk,nlogπk(xn∣x<n),ϕk∗∈arg⁡minϕk​ℒk​(ϕk).\begin{gathered}\mathcal{L}_{k}(\phi_{k})=-\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{D}_{k}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}m_{k,n}\log\pi_{k}(x_{n}\mid x_{<n}),\\ \phi_{k}^{\ast}\in\arg\min_{\phi_{k}}\mathcal{L}_{k}(\phi_{k}).\end{gathered} (5)

The mask selects prediction targets; all retained tokens remain causal context. In training and inference, WeAct retains the initial task and latest five user/tool messages, replacing older observation bodies with placeholders. We provide a complete training example in Appendix A.1.

For j≠kj\neq k, ∇ϕjℒk=0\nabla_{\phi_{j}}\mathcal{L}_{k}=0: optimizing capability kk leaves ϕj\phi_{j} and θ0\theta_{0} unchanged, avoiding the shared-parameter interference in Eq. 3. Refreshing a capability updates only its adapter factors, preserving the backbone and other modules’ parameters without data replay, as in the Writing refresh in Section 4.5.2.

2.3 Tool-Mediated Weight Actions

Separate adapters require a way to select capabilities as task needs change. We expose weight selection through native tool calls, reusing the model’s learned tool selection and argument generation without a separately trained router. This interface fits existing tool harnesses and lets new capabilities enter through registry entries.

Our harness extends MiroFlow (Su et al., 2026) with two MCP tools, load_lora and offload_lora. Both take a registry alias, lora_name, as their argument. Each call aa and result rr extend the history, h←h⊕a⊕rh\leftarrow h\oplus a\oplus r. After validation and successful execution, load/offload calls update the active index:

zt′={k,at=Load(k),zt=∅,∅,at=Offload(k),zt=k,zt,otherwise.z_{t}^{\prime}=\begin{cases}k,&a_{t}=\operatorname{Load}(k),\ z_{t}=\varnothing,\\ \varnothing,&a_{t}=\operatorname{Offload}(k),\ z_{t}=k,\\ z_{t},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (6)

Thus switching from ii to jj releases ii before loading jj. External, failed, rejected, and idempotent calls leave ztz_{t} unchanged; reloading the active alias or offloading an empty state is a no-op. The harness checks aliases, lifecycle rules, and policy constraints, returning status, errors, or stage guidance. These changes to the weights governing subsequent generation are Weight-level Internal Actions.

The policies differ in invocation timing. Under WeAct-soft, the base selects a module and the active module releases control, with revisits subject to coverage, repetition, and termination constraints. WeAct-hard prescribes adapter use in the same agent, by default LoRA-plan→\toLoRA-search→\toLoRA-write. The harness advances when the active stage emits an exit call, exhausts its budget, or reaches the no-tool threshold, recording release/load exchanges and handling termination or base-model fallback. Algorithm 1 outlines both.

Both control policies use the same execution mechanism: load and offload calls activate and release adapters that remain resident on the GPU, avoiding repeated host-to-device transfers. Weight changes require rebuilding the KV cache from the retained history under the new weights (Appendix B.3); answer-ready latency remains lower than Full SFT in the controlled evaluation (Section 4.4). The same tool interface also supports new capabilities: registering a new adapter with an alias and a capability description makes it available for selection, as in the Code insertion in Section 4.5.1.

3 Understanding Capability Separation

Learning heterogeneous capabilities through shared parameters, can erode earlier gains. Training separate LoRAs isolates their updates, but static fusion can alter each specialist’s effects during execution. We use controlled retention and fusion diagnostics to examine these two sources of interference and motivate WeAct’s capability-aligned parameter partitioning during learning and separate adapter selection during execution.

3.1 Capability Interference and Retention

We test whether shared updates erode earlier capabilities (Eq. 3). Plan, Search, and Writing define successive trajectory stages; sequential training models capability-specific fine-tuning after initial SFT (Section 4.5), as in sequential continual LoRA learning (Wang et al., 2025).

On frozen Qwen3-32B, we train these capabilities in all six orders under identical data and schedules. Shared LoRAs of rank 32 or 96 match the active rank or total parameter count of three rank-32 adapters, testing whether extra capacity suffices. The partitioned adapters are assigned by capability, as in WeAct, or randomly per trajectory, testing whether separation suffices without capability alignment.

Capability-aligned adapters remain unchanged during later stages, providing a fixed reference for capability drift. We report teacher-forced top-1 content-token accuracy on 168 validation trajectories, with a separate 24-trajectory monitoring subset (one seed; Appendix C); gradient diagnostics are in Appendix D.

The shared adapter matching the library’s total parameter count has a mean absolute accuracy loss of 1.67% across capabilities; extra capacity does not reduce this loss (Table 7). Writing gains least initially yet loses 49.2% of that gain (Figure 3). Random partitioning still incurs a mean absolute accuracy loss of 1.12%, so separation without capability alignment does not prevent forgetting.

3.2 Capability Mismatch under Static Fusion

We test whether static fusion preserves a fixed library of Plan, Search, and Writing specialists, each trained on its own capability. Full Additive sums their updates without final rank compression; TIES (Yadav et al., 2023), DARE-TIES (Yu et al., 2024; Yadav et al., 2023), and TSPA (Li et al., 2026c) produce rank-64 updates. The reference, Individual, selects the adapter matching each record’s capability label. We reserve 200 records per capability as validation data and measure paired mean target-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) gaps under teacher forcing (fusion minus Individual). We also measure local mismatch through (Δ​Wm−Δ​Wk)​h(\Delta W_{m}-\Delta W_{k})h on the same input activation hh, where Δ​Wm\Delta W_{m} is the merged update and Δ​Wk\Delta W_{k} is the individual adapter update for capability kk. For Full Additive, this difference is exactly the combined contribution of the other capability adapters. Validation data and metric details are in Appendix E.

None of the tested fusions eliminates the mean NLL degradation on any of the three capabilities (Figure 14). Local mismatch persists across LoRA layers in all three capabilities (Figure 13). Full Additive exhibits this mismatch despite retaining all updates without rank compression. Thus, combining intact updates can alter a specialist’s local effect through contributions from other capabilities. These results support preserving the specialists as separate updates and selecting them at runtime.

4 Experiments

We evaluate WeAct on eight deep-research benchmarks, then analyze evidence use in execution traces and training and inference efficiency. We also test capability insertion and local updates to assess modular continual adaptation.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Model and adapters. Weight-adaptation experiments start from Qwen3-32B (Yang et al., 2025): LoRA methods freeze the backbone; Full SFT updates it. Prompting baselines use the original checkpoint. The main WeAct library contains LoRA-plan, LoRA-search, and LoRA-write with ranks 32, 64, and 32. Single LoRA uses rank 128, matching the combined parameter count of the three separately trained adapters; static merges use rank 64. Only capability expansion uses LoRA-code. Other training and deployment settings, including learning rates and epochs, are in Appendix F.

Training data. We combine public agent trajectories from MiroVerse-v0.1 (Team et al., 2025) with supplementary trajectories generated from OpenSeeker-v1-Data (Du et al., 2026b) questions using our execution framework. Each LoRA adapter’s training samples retain execution context and supervise only its capability-specific outputs and handoff (Sec. 2.2). Appendix A summarizes data sources and construction; continual adaptation studies describe additional Code and Writing data.

Benchmarks. We cover general tool use, multi-hop evidence composition, and web research. General uses GAIA (Mialon et al., 2024); Multi-Hop QA comprises 2WikiMultiHopQA (Ho et al., 2020), Bamboogle (Press et al., 2023), and MuSiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022). Search comprises WebWalkerQA (Wu et al., 2025), xbench-DeepSearch (xbench Team, 2025), BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025), and FRAMES (Krishna et al., 2025), covering web navigation, retrieval, hard-to-find facts, and multi-source integration.

4.2 Main Results

Table 1 compares four adaptation mechanisms: prompting and multi-agent orchestration (ReAct (Yao et al., 2023), Least-to-Most (Zhou et al., 2023a), and ManuSearch (Huang et al., 2025)); unified adaptation (Full SFT, Single LoRA); static fusion (TIES-Merging (Yadav et al., 2023), DARE-TIES (Yu et al., 2024; Yadav et al., 2023), and TSPA (Li et al., 2026c); Appendix E); and WeAct-hard/soft. Multi-agent methods keep their own context and model-call structures. Static fusion and WeAct share one capability library, fused into a fixed update or selected at runtime.

WeAct-hard has the highest average, 45.47%, an accuracy gain of 2.67 points over Full SFT, and ranks first on six benchmarks. WeAct-soft has the second-highest average (43.21%) and leads on GAIA and MuSiQue. The hard result supports independent LoRA learning with prescribed, stepwise invocation for reliable adapter use within one agent. Soft flexibly schedules independently trained LoRAs within the harness’s runtime constraints.

Both variants outperform every static merge on all eight benchmarks; WeAct-hard also outperforms Single LoRA on all eight, and WeAct-soft on seven. Compared with Single LoRA, hard and soft achieve average-accuracy gains of 6.74% and 4.48%. The strongest static merge averages 35.66%, below Single LoRA’s 38.73%: these rank-64 fusions of the independently trained adapters, whose ranks sum to 128, perform worse than direct rank-128 training. This gap is consistent with the fusion mismatch in Section 3.2.

4.3 Search Effectiveness

To assess search effectiveness beyond answer accuracy, we apply SearchAtlas (Sang et al., 2026) to all ten methods on the same 100 tasks, producing 1,000 evidential query graphs. Query utilization (↑\uparrow) measures the fraction of issued queries on an evidence path to the answer; constraint coverage (↑\uparrow), the fraction of question constraints represented in those queries; and PK→\rightarrowanswer (↓\downarrow), the share of answers with content attributed to prior knowledge without retrieved support. Figure 4 reports the results; Appendix G gives formal definitions, graph construction, and task selection.

WeAct-hard ranks first and WeAct-soft second on all three metrics, ahead of Full SFT and the other baselines. Although ManuSearch issues the most queries, its answer-supporting queries cover only 39% of question constraints, versus 60% for WeAct-hard. These results show that WeAct connects search more effectively to answer support: a larger share of queries contributes to the answer, and those queries cover more question constraints. Fewer answers contain unsupported content attributed to prior knowledge.

4.4 Training and Inference Efficiency

Training compute. We assess WeAct’s training efficiency. With the same Qwen3-32B backbone and fewer epochs per adapter, WeAct uses 142.8 nominal EFLOPs, below Full SFT’s training compute, while achieving higher average accuracy. We count repeated contexts, epochs, packing, dense operations, and causal attention, with 1.23×\times Full SFT’s token exposure. LoRA omits frozen-backbone weight gradients. Across unequal capability segments, 2.06×\times token exposure at 0.95×\times per-token compute yields 1.96×\times total compute relative to Single LoRA with matched total trainable parameters (Appendix B.1). These results support efficient training of independent capability adapters.

Inference efficiency. Figure 5 pairs Table 1 Search accuracy with historical mean cumulative model-path time on the same server with the same concurrency, harness, and tool conditions, including retries; General/Multi-hop QA appear in Figure 8 (Appendix B.2). Against Single LoRA, WeAct-soft is more accurate and faster on six benchmarks; hard improves accuracy on eight and time on seven. Across 50 runs per method on prespecified WebWalkerQA tasks with identical hardware and task concurrency one, soft and hard reduce mean answer-ready latency by 33.4% and 20.3% versus Full SFT; soft is within 1% of Single LoRA. Model and tool execution dominate; adapter control and cache handling occupy 8.2%/2.8% of soft/hard time (Appendix B.3). These results support accuracy gains with modest switching overhead and net latency savings.

4.5 Modular Continual Adaptation

We assess catastrophic forgetting and modular continual adaptation: expanding and refining the library while retaining existing capabilities. We first evaluate general-capability retention with external tools disabled (Appendix H), then examine Code insertion and a local Writing refresh.

4.5.1 Continual Capability Expansion

To add code computation, we train a new LoRA-code adapter on MiroVerse-MegaScience trajectories converted to our tool and handoff protocol, keeping the base and existing adapters fixed without replay. Table 2 shows that inserting LoRA-code can improve accuracy on in-domain MegaScience and on SciBench (Wang et al., 2024a), without degrading DS-1000 (Lai et al., 2023) or GAIA (Mialon et al., 2024). Code insertion thus extends the library without retraining or harming existing capabilities (Appendix I).

4.5.2 Adapting to Evolving Writing Tasks

We test whether updating a single capability improves system-level report quality while preserving the rest of the library’s parameters. We continue training the existing LoRA-write adapter on trajectories synthesized in our harness from the OpenScholar (Asai et al., 2026) subset of DR Tulu (Shao et al., 2026) SFT data, replacing it with LoRA-write++. The base stays frozen, Plan and Search remain bitwise unchanged, and no historical data are replayed.

Table 3 shows gains on ResearchQA (Yifei et al., 2026) and DeepResearchBench (Du et al., 2026a) under hard and soft routing: hard gains 2.40 and 1.21 points, respectively. Both variants improve all four DRB dimensions, with soft gaining most in readability and instruction following (Appendix J, Table 11). Balancing new and historical Writing requirements within one module enables refinement without jointly retraining other capabilities. These gains support replay-free improvement without overwriting the backbone or other capability parameters.

5 Related Work

Deep-Research Agent Training. WebSailor-V2 and Tongyi DeepResearch improve agent training through synthetic data and post-training (Li et al., 2026a; Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2026). Step-DeepResearch and MiroThinker further organize learning around atomic capabilities (Hu et al., 2025; MiroMind Team et al., 2026). These methods share parameters across capabilities, coupling subsequent updates. Separating trainable parameters allows local refinement without updating the remaining library; WeAct realizes this organization as callable adapters over a frozen backbone.

Multi-Agent Orchestration. ManuSearch delegates planning, search, and reading to specialized agents; Chain of Agents distributes long contexts across workers (Huang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024). Their handoffs require intermediate messages and a manager to integrate the workers’ outputs. In WeAct, moving control between capability weights on a shared backbone offers another form of specialization: each selected policy continues from the same interaction history.

Multi-LoRA Composition and Routing. Early work such as LoRAHub and MoLE established reusable adapter composition (Huang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024). LD-MoLE learns token-dependent layerwise gates (Zhuang et al., 2026); LoGo selects and merges adapters per input without additional training (Lee et al., 2026). These methods focus on combining experts for task inputs rather than managing capability handoffs during an evolving agent trajectory. Adaptive Minds keeps the base model in control when calling adapters as tools (Shekar and Krishnan, 2026), whereas WeAct transfers control to the selected adapter. Macaron-V1 selects specialists per user turn (Mind Lab et al., 2026). Building on these approaches, WeAct couples independent capability learning with explicit handoffs within an agent trajectory. Selected adapters control reasoning and external tool use from shared history until offloading.

6 Discussion

Research on preserving specialization spans the frozen columns of early Progressive Neural Networks (Rusu et al., 2016) and the separate reasoning and tool-use LoRAs of recent DART (Li et al., 2026b). Our capacity-matched and random-partition controls show that capability alignment matters beyond capacity; fixed-library diagnostics reveal local fusion mismatch even without rank compression (Section 3). These results distinguish preserving learned parameters from preserving their functional effects during composition. Together with LoRA memory analysis (Back et al., 2026), they support aligning modules with independent update needs and selecting intact adapters as execution demands. Internal actions make this principle operational: newly trained LoRAs can enter an existing agent through the same interface. This suggests modular continual learning, with retention within updated modules remaining open.

7 Conclusion

We presented WeAct, which learns heterogeneous capabilities in independent LoRAs over a frozen backbone and switches active weights through internal actions within a shared agent trajectory. Controlled diagnostics support capability-aligned training and runtime selection for preserving specialization. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, WeAct improves average accuracy over Full SFT with lower nominal training compute. Code insertion expands the library with stable performance, and Writing refresh improves report quality. These results support independently learning agent capabilities and switching between them during execution, with potential for modular continual learning.

Limitations

Extending WeAct to sustained continual learning raises open questions about routing capacity and capability boundaries. It remains unclear how many adapters the agent can reliably distinguish and invoke as the library grows, and how well it can sustain longer sequences of internal actions. Repeated module insertion or refinement may also change capability selection, even when the rest of the library remains fixed. When task boundaries are unclear, general abilities such as reasoning may be needed across multiple stages, making it difficult to define separate LoRA modules and determine when each should be active. Whether incremental adapter expansion can improve these abilities while preserving performance on existing tasks remains an open question.

Appendix A Training Data Sources and Capability Segmentation

The training corpus contains 6,962 source trajectories before capability-specific splitting: 5,887 from MiroVerse-v0.1 (Team et al., 2025) and 1,075 generated from OpenSeeker-v1-Data (Du et al., 2026b) questions using our execution framework (Table 4).

Full-SFT and capability training data. Full SFT uses all 6,962 whole trajectories, covering all capabilities and retaining the five most recent tool responses. For WeAct, capability-specific splitting yields 6,962 Plan, 7,437 Search, and 6,962 Writing samples, with 200 samples per capability reserved for validation. Each sample retains the preceding execution context and supervises only the selected capability’s assistant outputs and terminal offload call. The activation call and result belong to the masked prefix; all tool feedback is also masked from the loss.

Capability labels follow the stage’s purpose (Section 2.2): Plan sets the goals and retrieval agenda; Search retrieves evidence, inspects sources, and cross-checks claims; Writing synthesizes the supported answer. A span may include several assistant/tool turns. The MiroVerse export separates planning before the first search from the subsequent search interaction and final answer synthesis. For continual adaptation, Code expansion extracts 3,413 code-computation samples from MiroVerse-MegaScience, with 200 reserved for validation; Writing refresh constructs 1,000 continuation samples from the OpenScholar subset of DR-Tulu SFT data (Asai et al., 2026; Shao et al., 2026). These maintenance corpora are separate from the initial three adapters’ data.

Train–test overlap. MiroVerse does not document the original splits of its sources, so we check overlap at the task level. We compare the task text of all 6,962 training trajectories with every evaluation question of the eight benchmarks. No evaluation question appears verbatim after normalization. A lexical screen flags questions with at least half of their IDF-weighted content words in a single training task whose trajectory also contains the gold answer; manual review of the flagged pairs finds overlap only through decomposed sub-agent subtasks. For 63 of the 2,417 MuSiQue questions (2.6%), the answer-bearing sub-question appears with the same answer as a training subtask, and 19 of these restate the full question with the bridge entity resolved. One WebWalkerQA question and one 2Wiki question show similar overlap; GAIA, Bamboogle, XBench-DS, BrowseComp, and FRAMES show none. Removing the 63 MuSiQue questions lowers each method’s MuSiQue accuracy by 0.04–0.47 points and leaves the ranking unchanged. The screen does not detect paraphrases below its threshold.

A.1 A Search Training Example

Figure 6 shows a Search training sample for identifying which Republican candidates elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 2008 previously served in the Minnesota House of Representatives. The boxed xx contains the system and user prompts, the Plan stage, and the Search loading exchange. It ends with the Search activation response, shown in full with headings and numbering added for readability. The boxed yy starts with the first Search assistant message and includes all five external exchanges and the final offload exchange. Its assistant tokens supply the targets in Eq. 5; xx and all tool feedback have zero loss. With keep_tool_result=5, the three tool returns in this prefix are all retained. Long contents and external-call arguments are abbreviated while all 20 messages remain visible.

A.2 Sensitivity to Capability Definitions and Annotation Rules

We explored capability definitions with GPT-5.4, starting from Retrieval, Reasoning, Verification, Plan, Code, and Writing. Paired comparisons use identical trajectories and assistant messages; changes count label-set differences, excluding boundary shifts within a label (Table 5).

Fine-grained labels and competing definitions. Separate Code from retrieval. Prioritizing execution increased Code and reduced Retrieval assignments. Absorb retrieval into Plan or Verification. Revised definitions shifted assignments between these labels, sometimes leaving aggregate counts unchanged. Isolate State Recap. Recapping known facts and gaps overlapped with ongoing evidence gathering; narrowing recap and broadening verification changed many assignments. Replace recap with Evidence Collection. This category remained ambiguous with Verification: identical lookups could be labeled as gathering details or checking a candidate.

Granularity and category-specific rules. Sparse labeling left nearly all messages unlabeled. Whole-turn labels recovered coverage; block-level labels also allowed opening plans and tool actions to be separated. Browse-oriented rules increased Verification on MiroVerse but reduced it on DR-Tulu while increasing Plan, indicating policy sensitivity rather than annotation accuracy. Introduce a Math capability. Math received only one span in each larger MiroVerse and DR-Tulu batch, offering little support for a separate module in this corpus.

Resulting capability design. We retain Plan, Search, Writing, and Code for choosing goals and actions, acquiring and checking external evidence, synthesizing answers, and executing computations. Unify external-evidence operations as Search. Evidence collection, source inspection, and verification share one capability, avoiding adapter assignments based on how a lookup is phrased. The main-table library uses Plan, Search, and Writing; Code is tested separately through capability insertion. The initial merged Search variant covered fewer tool-call blocks than its predecessor. Structural search candidates and text-anchored boundaries were still needed to recover coverage. These annotation findings motivate the chosen capabilities and segmentation procedure.

Appendix B Training and Inference Efficiency Details

B.1 Nominal Training Compute

All recipes use the same Qwen3-32B backbone and a maximum sequence length of 32k. Single LoRA matches the three adapters’ total trainable parameters: rank 128 versus ranks 32/64/32 on the same target projections. Plan, Search, and Writing train for two, three, and three epochs, respectively; Single LoRA trains for three and Full SFT for five. We account for each recipe’s actual token exposure and sequence lengths.

We count major matrix operations in Qwen3-32B training, with two FLOPs per multiply-add. Let DmD_{m} count processed token positions and QmQ_{m} estimate the sum of squared unpadded sequence lengths for recipe mm. With dense weights PP, rank-rr adapter weights PrP_{r}, LL layers, and total query width aa,

FFull=6​P​DFull+6​L​a​QFull,Fm=(4​P+6​Prm)​Dm+6​L​a​Qm,FWeAct=∑m∈{plan,search,writing}Fm,P=31.984×109,Pr=8.546×106r,L=64,a=8192.\begin{gathered}F_{\mathrm{Full}}=6PD_{\mathrm{Full}}+6LaQ_{\mathrm{Full}},\\ F_{m}=(4P+6P_{r_{m}})D_{m}+6LaQ_{m},\\ F_{\mathrm{WeAct}}=\!\sum_{m\in\{\mathrm{plan,search,writing}\}}F_{m},\\ P=31.984\times 10^{9},\quad P_{r}=8.546\times 10^{6}r,\\ L=64,\quad a=8192.\end{gathered} (7)

In FFullF_{\mathrm{Full}}, 6​P​DFull6PD_{\mathrm{Full}} counts forward, input-gradient, and weight-gradient products; in FmF_{m}, 4​P​Dm4PD_{m} omits frozen weight gradients; 6​Prm​Dm6P_{r_{m}}D_{m} trains the adapter; the shared 6​L​a​Qm6LaQ_{m} term counts causal query–key and attention–value products in both passes; FWeActF_{\mathrm{WeAct}} sums the three independently trained capability adapters’ costs; PP sums dense matrix sizes; PrP_{r} sums rank-rr factor sizes, including the output head; LL and aa are Qwen3-32B’s layer count and total query width.

Token exposure includes repeated contexts and epochs. Packed padding contributes to dense operations; block-diagonal attention uses individual unpadded trajectories. Length statistics retain the training text format, including reasoning; Single LoRA’s squared-length sum is estimated from randomized batch-token variance. Tool-call learning is part of adapter training; no separate router is trained. We exclude elementwise operations, optimizer updates, activation recomputation, communication, and I/O. Figure 7 shows length-statistic uncertainty as 95% bootstrap intervals for Single LoRA and Full SFT and summed component sensitivity bounds for WeAct.

WeAct uses 142.8 EFLOPs, 7.3% below Full SFT, despite processing 1.23×\times as many tokens (Figure 7). Relative to Single LoRA, 2.06×\times token exposure at 0.95×\times the per-token cost gives 1.96×\times total compute. Independent capability training thus costs less than Full SFT under these recipes, while its greater token exposure raises total compute over Single LoRA. These estimates use each recipe’s actual sequence lengths and padding, rather than measuring hardware throughput.

B.2 Historical Inference Efficiency

Records and timing. This analysis uses the logged runs behind the main results, collected over time on the same server with the same concurrency, harness, and tool conditions; we call them historical runs. The quality–time analysis covers six methods on eight benchmarks. The wall-time ECDFs additionally include ManuSearch, whose BrowseComp logs are unavailable, and use all 37,928 task-level records with valid timing. For each task and attempt, the first run is retry 0 and the final run is the highest retry index. Accuracy uses the final run’s judgment, and cost sums all runs up to it. Figures 5 and 8 pair these times with the accuracy in Table 1.

Model-path time is the union of model-call intervals within a run, summed across retries. Task-record wall time spans the logged task start and end and can include post-answer judging, so it measures logged execution time rather than answer-ready latency. The ECDFs include successful, failed, and anomaly-flagged records with valid timing, with one curve per method and benchmark.

Quality–model-path time comparisons. On GAIA, WeAct-soft improves accuracy over Single LoRA from 35.9% to 46.6% while reducing mean model-path time from 774.9 to 364.1 seconds; WeAct-hard reaches 40.8% at 181.0 seconds (Figure 8). TIES-R64 has shorter model paths on Multi-hop QA but lower accuracy than both WeAct variants on all eight benchmarks.

Typical cost and long tails. Both WeAct variants have lower mean task-record wall time than Full SFT on all eight benchmarks and lower means than Single LoRA on six and seven benchmarks for soft and hard, respectively. ReAct and TIES-R64 often have shorter typical runs, but WeAct has much shorter tails (Figure 9). On GAIA, their medians are lower than both WeAct variants’, yet WeAct-hard’s 99th percentile is below those of all four baselines.

On Multi-hop QA, ReAct and TIES-R64 also have shorter typical runs, while WeAct is more accurate than both and uses less mean wall time than Full SFT and Single LoRA. The largest tails occur on Search: on WebWalkerQA, WeAct-hard’s 99th percentile is 1,092 seconds versus ReAct’s 25,315 seconds, despite a longer median. XBench-DS shows the same contrast, although Single LoRA has a lower mean than WeAct-hard at lower accuracy. On the seven benchmarks with ManuSearch logs, both WeAct variants have lower mean and median wall time than ManuSearch. Thus the mean-time gains coexist with longer typical runs than some baselines and substantially shorter extreme runs.

Retries and first-run performance. Table 6 reports the share of tasks with saved retries on GAIA, 2Wiki, and WebWalkerQA. WeAct-soft retries more tasks than WeAct-hard, particularly on WebWalkerQA. WeAct-hard retries fewer tasks than the three trained baselines, and its accuracy changes by at most 0.15 percentage points from first to final run. By comparison, Single LoRA’s GAIA accuracy rises from 28.2% to 35.9%.

For WeAct-hard, the model-path time advantage over Single LoRA is already present in first runs on GAIA and 2Wiki. On WebWalkerQA, WeAct-hard uses 0.94×\times Single LoRA’s first-run time, compared with 0.65×\times when retries are included, so most of that gap comes from retries. The logs do not identify the cause of each retry.

B.3 Runtime Decomposition and Cache Costs

We evaluate Full SFT, Single LoRA, WeAct-hard, and WeAct-soft on the same prespecified WebWalkerQA tasks, with 50 runs per method on the same hardware at task concurrency one. All runs are included regardless of correctness. Answer-ready time spans the complete root-agent execution, excluding subsequent judging. We partition this interval into mutually exclusive model, external-tool, adapter-control, observed cache, answer-extraction, and setup/orchestration intervals; their sum equals the root duration for every run. Model time is further separated by the active adapter or base route. Identified cache intervals, covering the observed cache flush and post-switch prefill, are moved out of their enclosing model calls so that no time is counted twice.

Colors show the mean composition within each stage, not a single run’s event order. For WeAct-hard, the stages are Plan, Search, and a final Writing or Base stage. For WeAct-soft, Plan spans its load–offload interval, Search runs from the Plan offload to the Writing load (or to the end when Writing is absent), and Writing covers the remainder; these stages include Base calls and tools and average 16.2, 100.0, and 42.5 seconds, respectively. Terminal extraction, the startup Base interval, and Base-only execution are shown separately.

Figure 10 shows that WeAct-soft’s mean latency is close to Single LoRA’s, while both WeAct variants use less time than Full SFT. Adapter control and observed cache intervals together occupy 8.2% of soft’s time and 2.8% of hard’s. Time is attributed to the model that served each request, so base-model and external-tool time within a Search stage is not counted as Search-adapter time.

For the ManuSearch reference, we use 50 first-attempt runs without retries on the same task set, after checking that the question text matches. External tools account for 85.6% of its mean answer-ready time and model calls for 14.2%; extraction or summarization performed inside a tool counts as tool time. The figure breaks its tool bar between 425 and 2,120 seconds, using the same scale on both sides.

Appendix C Sequential Capability Retention

Adapter organizations. All four organizations start from frozen Qwen3-32B with identical initial weights. The shared baselines train one LoRA of rank 32 or 96, and the partitioned libraries train three rank-32 adapters. The capability partition gives each capability its own adapter in every trajectory. The random partition draws a fixed capability-to-adapter permutation for each trajectory, balanced across trajectories and kept for training and evaluation, so every adapter receives data from all three capabilities. A uniform rank isolates how parameters are organized; the main library uses capability-specific ranks (Section 4.1).

Data. We use 384 training and 192 validation trajectories, partitioning the latter into 168 for stage-end evaluation and 24 for monitoring. For each trajectory and capability, a fixed hash selects one complete assistant message as the target. The message is split into chunks of at most 512 target tokens, each with up to 7,168 preceding tokens of context; longer contexts keep the initial and most recent tokens around an omission marker. Each chunk with its context forms one training window.

Optimization. LoRA is applied to all attention and feed-forward projections with α=r\alpha=r and no dropout. Trainable parameters and optimizer moments are kept in FP32 over the BF16 backbone. Each order runs 288 updates, 96 per stage, with six windows per update; all organizations and orders consume the same window streams. We use AdamW without weight decay or gradient clipping, a linear warmup over the first 16 updates to 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}, and a constant rate afterwards. Optimizer state persists across stages, and adapters inactive in a stage receive no updates. All 24 runs (four organizations by six orders) use one training seed, so the six orders are experimental conditions rather than replicates.

Evaluation. Content-token accuracy is teacher-forced top-1 accuracy on the target tokens, excluding special tokens. We pool tokens within each message and weight trajectories equally. We evaluate the 168-trajectory validation subset before training and at the end of each stage (steps 0, 96, 192, and 288); the separate 24-trajectory subset is used only for the monitoring curves in Figure 11. Let Ak0A_{k}^{0}, AkownA_{k}^{\mathrm{own}}, and AkfinalA_{k}^{\mathrm{final}} be the validation accuracy of capability kk before training, at the end of its own stage, and after all stages. Averaging each over validation trajectories and over the four orders in which kk precedes another capability, we compute the fraction of acquired gain lost, FkF_{k}:

Fk=Akown−AkfinalAkown−Ak0.F_{k}=\frac{A_{k}^{\mathrm{own}}-A_{k}^{\mathrm{final}}}{A_{k}^{\mathrm{own}}-A_{k}^{0}}. (8)

The ratio is computed from averaged accuracies rather than averaged over trajectories. Table 7 reports its denominator (acquired gain), numerator (lost gain), and value.

Retention during later stages. Figure 11 follows the first capability of each order on the monitoring trajectories. Writing falls to about 55–70% of its gain within the first few checkpoints of the next stage, whereas Plan keeps roughly 80–95% throughout. Search loses more while Writing is trained than while Plan is trained, and partly recovers when Plan training follows Writing. The shared and randomly partitioned organizations follow similar trajectories.

Appendix D Diagnostic Metrics for Capability Separation

First-order update analysis. Eq. 3 considers a step on a single capability. For joint training, let 𝒟1,…,𝒟K\mathcal{D}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{D}_{K} be the span datasets with sampling shares pkp_{k} and per-capability losses ℒkshared​(ω)\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{shared}}(\omega) over shared parameters ω\omega. A shared adapter minimizes ℒmixshared​(ω)=∑kpk​ℒkshared​(ω)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mix}}^{\mathrm{shared}}(\omega)=\sum_{k}p_{k}\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{shared}}(\omega) with gradient steps δω=−η∑kpkgk\delta\omega=-\eta\sum_{k}p_{k}g_{k}, where gk=∇ωℒkshared​(ω)g_{k}=\nabla_{\omega}\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{shared}}(\omega). Writing Δ​ℒi\Delta\mathcal{L}_{i} for the change in capability ii’s shared-adapter loss, the first-order approximation is

Δ​ℒi≈−η⁡(pi​‖gi‖2+∑j≠ipj​⟨gi,gj⟩).\Delta\mathcal{L}_{i}\approx-\eta\Bigl(p_{i}\left\lVert g_{i}\right\rVert^{2}+\textstyle\sum_{j\neq i}p_{j}\left\langle g_{i},\,g_{j}\right\rangle\Bigr). (9)

When ⟨gi,gj⟩≈0\left\langle g_{i},\,g_{j}\right\rangle\approx 0, the other capabilities’ updates give capability ii little first-order transfer, and its own term scales with pip_{i}, so unequal sampling shares or gradient norms let one capability dominate the mixed direction. Like Eq. 3, this describes one gradient step; with an adaptive optimizer, the realized update also depends on optimizer state.

Gradient measurements. For capability gradients gig_{i} and gjg_{j} in the same adapter parameter space, we report cos⁡(gi,gj)=⟨gi,gj⟩/(‖gi‖​‖gj‖)\cos(g_{i},g_{j})=\left\langle g_{i},\,g_{j}\right\rangle/(\left\lVert g_{i}\right\rVert\left\lVert g_{j}\right\rVert) and the norms ‖gi‖\left\lVert g_{i}\right\rVert. The norm ratio maxi⁡‖gi‖/mini⁡‖gi‖\max_{i}\left\lVert g_{i}\right\rVert/\min_{i}\left\lVert g_{i}\right\rVert is computed without weighting by sampling share, which enters through Eq. 9.

Figure 12 probes a jointly trained rank-96 Single LoRA (α=32\alpha=32) at ten evenly spaced training checkpoints, using the same pool of capability spans at every checkpoint. Most cosines remain positive, while the largest-to-smallest norm ratio grows over training; Writing has the smallest gradients after the first checkpoint. Positive cosines mean that, to first order, a step on one capability does not raise another’s loss. The loss in Section 3.1 arises under sequential training, where a capability that has already been fit has small gradients, so later updates can raise its loss through higher-order terms even without gradient conflict.

Appendix E Static-Merge Residual Details

E.1 Fixed Capability Library and Validation Data

We fix Qwen3-32B and the same independently trained Plan, Search, and Writing adapters throughout this diagnostic. Adapter ranks and scaling follow the main experimental setup (Appendix F). Individual activates the adapter matching the target capability. Full Additive sums the effective updates Δ​Wk=(αk/rk)​Bk​Ak\Delta W_{k}=(\alpha_{k}/r_{k})B_{k}A_{k} without final rank compression. TIES-R64, DARE-TIES-R64, and TSPA-R64 construct a fixed merged update and represent it at rank 64. TIES uses density 0.2; DARE-TIES additionally uses drop rate 0.5 and seed 0. We follow the original TSPA procedure (Li et al., 2026c), which performs attention alignment followed by LoRA parameter alignment. It optimizes rotations and scaling within the low-rank factors before merging the aligned adapters.

We use our capability-specific validation split: each capability’s source data is shuffled with seed 42, the first 200 records form each capability’s validation set, and the remainder is used for training. Both the activation and NLL diagnostics draw their evaluation records from these validation sets. We render their messages with the training format, preserving supervision masks, capability labels, and recorded tool observations. Evaluation replays the recorded text without making new external tool calls. The context and target selection rules for each diagnostic are described below.

E.2 Local Effects on Matched Activation

The activation diagnostic tests whether a static update preserves the local effect of the capability-specific update. For projection jj, we run Individual to obtain its input hk,jh_{k,j} and evaluate every candidate on that same input:

ρm,k,j=‖(Δ​Wm,j−Δ​Wk,j)​hk,j‖2max⁡(‖Δ​Wk,j​hk,j‖2,10−12).\rho_{m,k,j}=\frac{\|(\Delta W_{m,j}-\Delta W_{k,j})h_{k,j}\|_{2}}{\max\!\left(\|\Delta W_{k,j}h_{k,j}\|_{2},10^{-12}\right)}. (10)

Here mm identifies the merge rule, kk the target capability, and jj the LoRA projection; Δ​Wm,j\Delta W_{m,j} and Δ​Wk,j\Delta W_{k,j} are the merged and individual adapter updates, respectively. This measures adapter-induced local mismatch, excluding differences introduced by propagating each candidate’s own activations through later layers. For Full Additive, writing h=hk,jh=h_{k,j}, the difference is exactly the combined contribution of the other capability adapters:

(∑iΔ​Wi,j−Δ​Wk,j)​h=∑i≠kΔ​Wi,j​h.\textstyle\bigl(\sum_{i}\Delta W_{i,j}-\Delta W_{k,j}\bigr)h=\sum_{i\neq k}\Delta W_{i,j}h. (11)

The residual thus measures how non-target updates change the matched adapter’s local action; their contributions can partly reinforce or cancel one another.

We retain an 8,192-token prefix of each trajectory and select causally aligned supervised positions. The activation used to predict a target token is taken from the preceding position, with its capability label checked at that source position. Each validation record contributes four positions across all attention and feed-forward LoRA projections in every transformer layer. We average positions and projections within each layer and trajectory, then weight trajectories equally.

Figure 13 shows capability-dependent local mismatch across layers. Conflict handling and subspace alignment change its magnitude, and the ordering of the fusions varies by capability, but none recovers the matched update’s local effect for all three capabilities.

E.3 Target-Text Fit and Variation across Trajectories

We complement the local diagnostic with teacher-forced target-token NLL, comparing each static condition and Individual on the same record and supervised targets. LoRA updates are applied to all adapted layers, including the output head. Contexts are capped at 4,096 tokens, and each record contributes the mean NLL of the valid supervised tokens visible in its target capability span. For record xx with capability kk and merge rule mm, we compute

Δ​Lm,k​(x)=Lm​(x)−Lk​(x),\Delta L_{m,k}(x)=L_{m}(x)-L_{k}(x), (12)

where LL is the record’s mean target-token NLL. Figure 14 shows the distribution of these paired differences across validation records, with diamonds marking their equally weighted means; zero denotes equal target-text fit.

The mean NLL gap is positive for every tested fusion in all three capabilities, although some records have gaps close to zero or negative (Figure 14). Full Additive’s Writing mean exceeds its median, indicating that a subset of records with large gaps raises the mean. The tested fusions therefore reduce mean target-text fit, with the size and direction of the change varying across records.

The local and NLL diagnostics agree at the capability level: every tested fusion leaves local mismatch and poorer mean target-text fit relative to capability-matched use. These results support preserving the specialists as separate updates and selecting them at runtime. Section 4.2 reports the task-level effect of these merges.

Appendix F Experimental Setup Details

This appendix gives the configuration of the main experiments; the sequential diagnostic uses its own configuration (Appendix C).

Capability adapters. The capability adapters use ranks 32, 64, and 32 for Plan, Search, and Writing, with αk=32\alpha_{k}=32 and no LoRA dropout. Search uses rank 64 because rank-32 pilots showed repetitive, non-terminating reasoning and unreliable external-tool and offload_lora calls. Each adapter places low-rank factors on the query, key, value, and output projections and on the gate, up, and down projections of all 64 transformer layers, and on the output projection (lm_head); input embeddings are not adapted. We train the adapters with Tinker (Thinking Machines Lab, 2025) using the Qwen3 chat template, a batch size of eight, and a maximum sequence length of 32k. Adam uses (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.95)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95) and ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}, and the learning rate decays from its peak to zero on a cosine schedule without warmup. Plan trains for two epochs at a peak learning rate of 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}; Search and Writing train for three epochs at 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} and 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}, respectively. Each capability’s data are shuffled with seed 42, and the first 200 records form a validation set for NLL monitoring. The activation and NLL diagnostics draw their evaluation records from these validation sets (Appendix E). Samples for different modules can share source trajectories and execution prefixes, but not loss targets. Single LoRA follows the same recipe with rank 128, three epochs, and a peak learning rate of 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}.

Full SFT. The full-parameter baseline starts from the same Qwen3-32B checkpoint and is trained with LLaMA-Factory on eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs, using DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 without offloading, FlashAttention-2, Liger kernels, gradient checkpointing, and bfloat16. Each optimizer step uses 64 packed sequences: one per device per micro-step, with eight gradient-accumulation steps. AdamW uses a peak learning rate of 4×10−54\times 10^{-5}, warmup over the first 10% of steps followed by cosine decay, and no weight decay. Training runs for five epochs with seed 42. Trajectories are packed into 32k token sequences with block-diagonal attention, so packed trajectories do not attend to one another. The Qwen3 template keeps the reasoning content, and prompt and tool-response tokens are excluded from the loss. Full SFT trains on compressed trajectories (Appendix A).

Evaluation protocol. The main table reports each benchmark separately, and its Avg. column is the unweighted mean over the eight benchmarks. Each method keeps its own context management and model-call structure and attempts every task once. A task that ends without a valid boxed answer is retried up to twice, allowing at most three attempts; the first valid answer is scored. On 2Wiki, Bamboogle, and MuSiQue, an answer is correct if the boxed answer exactly matches the gold answer or one of its aliases after normalization (lowercasing and removing punctuation, articles, and extra whitespace). On the other five benchmarks, GPT-5.6 Luna compares the answer with the reference using each benchmark’s grading prompt; on GAIA, WebWalkerQA, and FRAMES, answers that match the reference after normalization are accepted without a judge call. For a benchmark with accuracy pp on nn evaluation tasks, Table 1 gives the nominal task-based binomial standard error p⁡(1−p)/n\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}. For Avg., we propagate these as ∑bSEb2/8\sqrt{\sum_{b}\mathrm{SE}_{b}^{2}}/8, treating benchmarks as independent.

Appendix G Trace Analysis Details

Graph construction. We use SearchAtlas’s released builder and evaluator to represent searches as query nodes, with page reads supplying evidence to the queries that retrieved them. Edges link queries, question constraints, prior knowledge, and the final answer. Attribution uses GPT-5.2 at temperature 0 with JSON outputs and access to all earlier tool results. Each question is decomposed once into constraint units shared across methods; evidence and answer attribution are performed separately for each method. Reader summaries are treated as observed content without checking the original pages.

Diagnostics. Let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be the issued queries, AA the answer, and 𝒬A⊆𝒬\mathcal{Q}_{A}\subseteq\mathcal{Q} the queries that reach AA through evidence-use edges. Let CC be the question’s constraint units, C⁡(q)⊆CC(q)\subseteq C those deployed by query qq, and EPKE_{\mathrm{PK}} the prior-knowledge edges. For nonempty query and constraint sets, the diagnostics used here are

QU=|𝒬A||𝒬|,\displaystyle\mathrm{QU}=\frac{|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|}{|\mathcal{Q}|}, (13)
Cov=|⋃q∈𝒬AC⁡(q)||C|,\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}=\frac{\left|\bigcup_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{A}}C(q)\right|}{|C|}, (14)
PKAans=[(PK,A)∈EPK].\displaystyle\mathrm{PKA}_{\mathrm{ans}}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[(\mathrm{PK},A)\in E_{\mathrm{PK}}\right]. (15)

QU measures the fraction of queries on an evidence path to the answer. Cov uses the constraints deployed by direct answer parents and their evidence ancestors, consistently across tasks. PKAans indicates an answer edge attributed to prior knowledge without retrieved support. Reported scores are task means, so mean PKAans is the share of answers with such an edge. Higher QU and Cov and lower PKAans indicate stronger retrieval grounding. Low coverage may indicate missing retrieval support for some question requirements; unsupported content is not necessarily incorrect.

Trajectories. Except as noted in Section 4.3, we use for each method and task the trajectory behind the corresponding result in Table 1: the earliest successful attempt for correctly answered tasks and the last completed attempt for tasks answered incorrectly.

Quality control and statistics. A task is excluded for all methods if any method’s graph contains CJK text (the constraint matching relies on English lexical signals), has no answer signals, or records an unrecovered constraint-arbitration error; excluded tasks are not replaced. The 100 retained tasks come from MuSiQue (23), 2Wiki (20), Bamboogle (18), GAIA (17), FRAMES (14), BrowseComp (4), and WebWalkerQA (4); xbench-DS tasks do not pass the language filter. Means weight tasks equally. Intervals are 95% percentile intervals from 5,000 task-level bootstrap resamples.

Additional observations. Table 8 reports the means in Figure 4. Both WeAct variants lead all baselines on the three diagnostics. ManuSearch issues the most queries, but WeAct-hard covers more question constraints along the evidence paths supporting its answers. WeAct-hard also has fewer tasks without a retrieval-supported answer path than any baseline.

Appendix H General Capability Preservation

We evaluate catastrophic forgetting on MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024b), IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023b), MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023), StructFlow, and HumanEval. All external tools are disabled: WeAct reasons through model weights while retaining internal adapter selection.

Table 10 shows that WeAct substantially mitigates the general-capability forgetting observed under Full SFT across these five benchmarks. Full SFT loses 11.60 and 15.16 points on MMLU-Pro and IFEval, respectively. Both WeAct variants exceed Base on MMLU-Pro and MT-Bench and remain close to it on StructFlow. IFEval still declines, but much less than under Full SFT; HumanEval matches Base under soft routing and declines less than Full SFT under hard routing. Both variants thus retain higher scores than Full SFT on every evaluated benchmark.

Remark 1.

With every adapter inactive, the model parameters are bitwise equal to the frozen base θ0\theta_{0}; with adapter kk active, they differ by Δ​θk\Delta\theta_{k}. This concerns parameters only; Table 10 measures behavior with adapters available.

Appendix I Code Insertion: Implementation and Evaluation Protocol

Insertion adds a code capability without retraining the base, modifying the plan, search, and writing adapters, or replaying their data. We train only a new code adapter on code-computation trajectories from MiroVerse-MegaScience, converted to our tool and handoff protocol; these trajectories use code to calculate and verify answers from given conditions. Registering the code alias extends the routing vocabulary from K=3K=3 to K=4K=4.

The evaluation has two parts. First, we compare hashes of the base and the three existing adapters before and after insertion. Second, as shown in Table 9, we evaluate the original GAIA tasks before and after insertion, reporting the paired quality change and how often code is invoked on tasks that need no computation (2 of 80). New-capability utility is measured on MegaScience (Fan et al., 2026), SciBench (Wang et al., 2024a), and DS-1000 (Lai et al., 2023). Insertion succeeds only if code tasks improve, the existing hashes are unchanged, old-task quality does not decrease, and misrouting into code stays low; unchanged parameters alone do not suffice.

Appendix J Writing Refresh: Protocol and Full Results

Local update. We continue training Writing on OpenScholar-based trajectories synthesized in our harness, keeping the base, Plan, and Search fixed and replaying no earlier data. The pool contains 1,000 rows from 983 unique trajectories. Splitting by trajectory ID gives 795 training rows and 205 validation rows; only the training split is used for the update.

Report-quality results. Table 11 gives the DRB rubric breakdown for the overall scores in Table 3. DRB totals use the evaluator’s weighted aggregation, not an unweighted rubric mean.

Auxiliary adaptation and retention probe. The paired teacher-forced probe uses identical reference sequences, tokenization, and masks for the original and refreshed Writing adapters. It activates Writing on Writing positions and uses the frozen base elsewhere. NLL is averaged over supervised tokens and exponentiated for perplexity; targets may include reasoning and tool calls as well as report text. Table 12 reports NLL and perplexity for the OpenScholar and historical Writing validation sets under this shared protocol.
